title: Check yourself: security practices in Java

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A shop refuses any product tag that contains `<` or `>`, and stores accepted tags as typed. The storefront applies NFKC to each tag before it inserts the tag into the page's HTML. A seller submits `＜b＞sale＜/b＞`, typed with the full-width brackets U+FF1C and U+FF1E. What happens?

options.text: The check accepts it and the storefront inserts `sale`, since the check reads the characters as typed and NFKC maps the full-width brackets to ASCII.
options.says: String.contains compares characters as they are; NFKC maps full-width forms such as ．／ to ASCII one layer later, after the check passed them.

options.text: The check accepts it as typed and the storefront inserts the full-width brackets as text, since NFKC maps letters and digits to ASCII but not brackets.
options.says: The run shows NFKC turning full-width ．．／ into ../: it maps full-width punctuation too.

options.text: The check refuses it, since `String.contains` applies NFKC before comparing, as the storefront does, so the full-width brackets match `<` and `>`.
options.says: String.contains never normalises: the deny-list accepted the full-width ../ in the run.

options.text: The check refuses it, since Java maps full-width characters to ASCII while decoding the request, before either the check or the storefront sees them.
options.says: The full-width input reached the deny-list unchanged and was accepted; only the later NFKC step turned it into ASCII.

origin.section: Validate the Value the Next Layer Will Use, Against an Allow-List

questions.stem: Invite codes used to come from `new Random(System.currentTimeMillis())`, one per request, and two guests got the same code. The fix creates one `new Random()` at start-up, with no seed, shared by every request; each code is its next `nextLong()` in hex. Is the fixed version fit for invite codes?

options.text: Yes, since the no-argument constructor draws its 48-bit seed from the operating system's entropy source, which its javadoc says makes its values unpredictable.
options.says: Leaving the seed out removes the collisions but not the formula; the javadoc says Random is not cryptographically secure, whatever its seed.

options.text: Yes, since the shared instance applies its linear congruential step to one seed taken at start-up, which its javadoc says keeps later values unpredictable.
options.says: Removing the collisions leaves the formula; the javadoc says Random is not cryptographically secure whatever its seed.

options.text: No, since the shared instance still advances a 48-bit seed by a linear congruential step, which its javadoc says is not cryptographically secure.
options.says: Random advances a 48-bit seed by a linear congruential step, and its javadoc says instances are not cryptographically secure.

options.text: No, since the no-argument constructor starts its 48-bit seed from one fixed default value, which its javadoc says repeats after every restart.
options.says: Leaving the seed out removes the collisions; the problem is the formula, not a fixed default seed.

origin.section: A Token from Random Is a Function of Its Seed; Use SecureRandom

questions.stem: So that tests can replay tokens, a service builds its generator with `SecureRandom.getInstance("SHA1PRNG")` and calls `setSeed(startTimeMillis)` before the first token, in production too. Two replicas start in the same millisecond. How do their tokens compare?

options.text: They issue the same tokens, since a `SHA1PRNG` seeded before its first use draws on that seed alone.
options.says: Two SHA1PRNG instances seeded with the same value before use returned the same output in the run.

options.text: They issue the same tokens, since `setSeed` on a `SecureRandom` replaces its state with the seed given.
options.says: The javadoc says setSeed supplements the seed, and two NativePRNG instances seeded alike gave different output.

options.text: They issue different tokens, since `setSeed` on a `SecureRandom` adds to the seed it took from the system.
options.says: That holds for NativePRNG; a SHA1PRNG that has produced nothing yet has no seed to add to, and repeated in the run.

options.text: They issue different tokens, since a `SHA1PRNG` seeded before its first use mixes in the system's entropy.
options.says: Two SHA1PRNG instances seeded alike before use returned the same output in the run, so nothing from the system was mixed in.

origin.section: A Token from Random Is a Function of Its Seed; Use SecureRandom

questions.stem: A batch job reads a database password into a `char[]`, passes `new String(pw)` to a client library's `login(String)`, which keeps no reference, and wipes the array in a `finally`. Before the next full garbage collection, an engineer writes a dump of the whole heap. Where in that dump is the password?

options.text: In the `String` only, since the wipe cleared the array, and the unreachable `String` stays in the heap until a collection reclaims it.
options.says: The run's dump 4: one copy as String bytes, none as char[], after the array was wiped; gone only after a full GC.

options.text: In the array and the `String`, since `Arrays.fill` wrote its zeros into a copy of the array, so the original array still holds the characters.
options.says: Arrays.fill overwrote the array itself: dump 3 shows no char[] copy after the wipe.

options.text: Nowhere, since the `String` shares the array's storage, so the wipe cleared both long before the next full garbage collection.
options.says: new String(p2) copied the characters into the String's own byte array; dump 4 still found them after the wipe.

options.text: Nowhere, since a dump of the whole heap writes out only the objects a live thread can still reach, so the unreachable `String` is skipped.
options.says: A whole-heap dump (liveOnly false) contained the unreachable String; only a live-only dump runs a full GC first.

origin.section: Wiping a char[] Removes Your Copy of a Secret; a String Copy Stays Until GC

questions.stem: `LoginRequest(String username, String password)` overrides `toString` to print `password=***`. A new endpoint builds `record PasswordChange(String username, String oldPassword, String newPassword)` from two such requests, declares no `toString` in it, and logs it when the change fails. What does the log line show?

options.text: Both passwords in clear, since the generated `toString` of `PasswordChange` prints each component the same way, whichever record its value came from.
options.says: A record's generated toString prints every component by name and value; the override protects one record only.

options.text: Both passwords in clear, since the generated `toString` of `PasswordChange` overrides the `LoginRequest` one for the values copied into it.
options.says: The LoginRequest override still works on LoginRequest; PasswordChange holds plain Strings, and its generated toString prints them without consulting any other record.

options.text: `***` for both, since the generated `toString` of `PasswordChange` hides each component whose name contains `password`.
options.says: The generated toString printed password=hunter2-example in the run; it hides nothing by name.

options.text: `***` for both, since the generated `toString` of `PasswordChange` reuses the `LoginRequest` override for values copied from it.
options.says: The override belongs to the LoginRequest type, not to the String values; only a type such as Secret carries the mask with the value.

origin.section: A Record's toString Prints Every Component, Password Included

concepts: A deny-list compares characters as typed, so percent-encoded and full-width spellings pass it and become the forbidden text one layer later.
An overridden toString protects one record; another record holding the same values as Strings prints them again, while a Secret type carries the mask with the value.
java.util.Random is a fixed formula of a 48-bit seed; a clock seed repeats tokens and leaving the seed out still leaves it not cryptographically secure.
A SHA1PRNG seeded before its first use repeats its output for the same seed, while NativePRNG mixes a seed into its own state.
Wiping a char[] removes that array's copy, but a String made from it cannot be overwritten and stays in the heap, and in a whole-heap dump, until a collection reclaims it.
